newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish finmin wants PLN 1 bln c.bank flood credit.
newsitem.headline: Polish finmin wants PLN 1 bln c.bank flood credit.

text.p: Poland's finance ministry wants to amend this year's budget law to allow the government to borrow around one billion zlotys from the central bank to deal with the floods in southern Poland, Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Monday.
Belka told a news conference the government also wanted the amended law to accommodate a $300 million loan from the World Bank for the same purpose.
"We are working on an amended version of the budget law so that parliament can vote on it on Wednesday," Belka said.

Many days of torrential rain in southern Poland over the last week have caused floods which already inundated 4,000 square kilometres, killing at least 36 and forcing tens of thousands out of their homes.
"We will first use the 500-700 million zlotys squeezed out of this year's budget...but we also want the new law to raise the limit of foreign loans by $300 million," Belka said.

"To avoid a situation in which there would be no money in the treasury's coffers we want the new budget law to allow the state to borrow some one billion zlotys from the National Bank of Poland," Belka said.

The government has already used up its 2.5 billion zloty limit for financing the budget deficit in the central bank this year and the finance ministry promised not to seek more loans from the NBP in line with Poland's new constitution.
However, the constitution, which forbids governments to borrow from the independent central bank, does not become effective until October.
Estimates of the flood damage will be known in mid-August but the government has already said the losses were huge.
Poland's parliament will break its summer recess and meet on Wednesday to listen to the government's report on the deluge and vote on how to raise funds to deal with it.

Analysts have said that of all methods of seeking funds to deal with the flood damage, borrowing from the central bank and taking a dollar-denominated loan from abroad were the worst scenarios from a monetary policy point of view.
"If the funds were raised through a national loan scheme or taxes, the operation would not boost money supply," a senior banking analyst, who asked not to be named, said.

"Raising the cash through central bank and foreign loans will increase money creation, force the central bank to sterilise the incoming currency and we can forget about ambitious inflation targets," he said.
